doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: New Orleans jazz's influence on Chicago style
summary: Smith explains how King Oliver, Freddie Keppard and slap bassist Bill Johnson shaped Chicago jazz, and wishes he could witness it.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: I’m glad you mentioned that because — is there a discernible difference between what happened to New Orleans jazz when it moved up to Chicago?

There sure is. The New Orleans players who kept playing it in Chicago influenced the people in Chicago. I think the Chicago tradition was largely a dance band — hotel bands, dance bands, ragtime players — and when King Oliver’s band went to Chicago, and before that Freddie Keppard with the Original Creole Band, they just showed a whole new way of playing. For instance I would doubt that there were a lot of bass players around Chicago who plucked the instrument. They probably bowed like every other bassist did, until Bill Johnson went there before World War I with Freddie Keppard and the Original Creole Band, and he was a sensation, and he had a feature number “Weary Blues” where he played chorus after chorus of slap string bass. So if you figure that’s 1911 or 1913, that would turn the whole town over. And I think the New Orleans, Oliver and Armstrong, Johnny Dodds, Jimmy Noone, Baby Dodds, each of those people, and Jelly Roll Morton, they’d have an influence on the Chicago style that I think set a real course for it until Earl Hines and Bix changed it again. But I think there probably wouldn’t be a “Chicago jazz” had it not been for the New Orleans players going there. Because that’s what really turned on a lot of the players. In interviews with Goodman and Sullivan and Tough and all those guys, they said, “Well my influence was —” and almost in every case it was New Orleans musicians.
Don’t you kind of wish you could go back in time and witness some of that interaction?
I’m ready. I’ll go right now.
Sometimes you feel like maybe you were born in the wrong era.
I feel that way about twenty hours a day.
